label: Saying goodbye to a pet

what_happens.title: What happens when a pet dies
goals: Died means the body stopped working and cannot start again
It is nobody's fault in most cases
It is okay to feel very sad
what_happens.parentSkill: Use simple, true words: 'Our pet died. Its body stopped working. It cannot feel pain anymore, and it cannot come back.'

who_is_there.title: Who helps me
goals: Friends, teachers and others can help
who_is_there.parentSkill: Share your own sadness openly, so your child knows grief is normal.

what_i_do.title: What I do to say goodbye
goals: Say goodbye in my own way
Make a memory: a drawing, a letter, a flower
what_i_do.parentSkill: Offer a simple goodbye ritual and let your child choose how to take part.

if_scared.title: When the sadness is big
goals: Grief can feel sad, angry, worried or numb
Feelings come and go in waves
Calm tools: talking, crying, hugs, slow breaths
if_scared.parentSkill: Accept every feeling and do not rush it: 'You miss Pebble so much. I miss her too.'

rehearsal.title: Let's remember together
goals: Make a memory book or box
Choose a way to keep remembering
rehearsal.parentSkill: Make a memory page together tonight: a photo, a drawing and three words about the pet.

steps: A grown-up explains that the pet is very ill or has died
Talk about what died means: the body stopped working and cannot start again
Say goodbye, in person or in our own way
Have a small goodbye ritual, like planting a flower or making a picture
Remember happy times and look at photos
Feel the feelings, and talk about them
Keep the pet in our memories
sensory: a quiet house without the pet's sounds
the pet's empty bed or bowl
the smell of the pet on a blanket
honestyNotes: Use the real words 'died' and 'dead'; never say 'went to sleep', 'got lost' or 'went away', which confuse children and can make sleep or trips scary. Explain that the body stopped working and cannot come back. Never promise a new pet as a replacement. Grief has no timetable. Let the parent explain any family or faith beliefs about what happens after death.

No. When a body stops working, it cannot start again.
We can keep remembering, and that keeps our pet in our hearts.
No. It was not because of anything you did or did not do.
You loved your pet, and your pet knew it.
[[GROWNUP]] will tell you what you would like to know.
Now that it has died, it cannot feel any pain.
[[GROWNUP]] will tell you what our family believes.
Its body may be buried or cared for, and its memory is with us.

questionButtons.text: Why do I feel so sad?
fallbackAnswer: You feel sad because you loved your pet very much.
It is okay to cry, and the sadness gets softer with time.
Everyone dies one day, usually when they are very, very old.
[[GROWNUP]] plans to be here for a very long time, looking after you.

questionButtons.text: Can we get a new pet?
fallbackAnswer: Maybe one day, when the family feels ready.
A new pet would not replace our pet. It would be a new friend.
You can draw a picture, write a letter or plant a flower.
You choose what feels right.

questionButtons.text: Do I have to tell people?
fallbackAnswer: You can choose who to tell and when.
Telling a teacher can help them understand how you feel.

questionButtons.text: Is it okay to laugh and play?
fallbackAnswer: Yes. Laughing and playing does not mean you forgot.
Your pet would want you to be happy.

techniques.label: Using real words
techniques.how: Say 'died', not 'went to sleep' or 'went away'.

techniques.label: A memory box
techniques.how: Collect a photo, a toy and drawings in a box.

techniques.label: A goodbye ritual
techniques.how: Plant a flower or say a few words together.

techniques.label: Happy stories
techniques.how: Tell favourite and funny stories about the pet.

techniques.label: All feelings are okay
techniques.how: Accept sadness, anger, numbness and laughter.

techniques.label: Telling school
techniques.how: Let the teacher know so they can be gentle.

techniques.label: A letter to the pet
techniques.how: Write or draw a letter saying goodbye.

techniques.label: Hugs and closeness
techniques.how: Offer extra hugs and time together.

techniques.label: Smell the flower, blow the candle
techniques.how: Breathe in slowly through the nose and out like blowing a candle.

sentences.text: [[CHILD]]'s pet has died, or is very ill and will die soon.
Died means the body stopped working.
The heart stopped beating, and the body stopped breathing.
A pet that has died cannot feel pain, hunger or cold anymore.
Before bed, here is a story about a little bear called Toby.
Toby had an old tortoise called Pebble.
Pebble had lived a very long time and grown very slow.
One morning, Mama Bear sat down with Toby.
She said, Pebble died in the night.
Her body was very old, and it stopped working.
She cannot feel anything now, not hungry, not cold, not sore.
Toby asked, will she wake up?
Mama held his paw and said gently, no, when someone dies they cannot come back.
Toby cried, and Mama cried too.
Tomorrow evening, the story goes on.
It cannot come back to life.
This is very sad, and it is okay to cry.
Pets often die because they are very old or very ill.
It is not because of anything anyone in the family did wrong.
[[CHILD]] can ask any question about it, and [[GROWNUP]] will answer honestly.

Other pets in the home may seem confused or quiet.
In the story, the whole bear family missed Pebble.
Papa Bear sat quietly and looked at her empty shell box.
Mama Bear's eyes were wet.
Even the cat, Whiskers, sniffed the box and lay beside it.
Toby's teacher, Mrs Owl, heard the news.
She said, I had a dog who died when I was little, and I missed him very much.
Toby's friend the rabbit said, my fish died last summer.
Grandpa Bear came over and told a funny story about Pebble eating a whole strawberry.
Everyone laughed a little, and cried a little.
Toby did not feel alone.
Tomorrow evening, the story goes on.
Friends and teachers can be told, so they understand.
Some friends have lost pets too.
Grandparents and other family can share memories.
Nobody has to be sad alone.

In the story, Toby the bear wanted to say goodbye to Pebble.
Mama asked, how would you like to say goodbye?
Toby drew a picture of Pebble eating a strawberry.
Then the family planted a little strawberry plant in the garden.
Papa said a few words: Pebble, you were slow and kind, and we loved you.
Toby put his drawing in a memory box with Pebble's favourite leaf.
Then everyone told a happy memory.
Toby said, I liked when she climbed on my foot.
Everyone smiled.
Toby felt sad, and a little bit warm inside.
Tomorrow evening, the story goes on.

Pebble's box was empty, and it made his chest feel heavy.
Will you die too, Mama, he asked.
Mama did not say, nobody will ever die.
Mama said, I plan to be here for a very, very long time, to look after you.
Toby cried, and Mama held him close.
The next day, Toby laughed while playing with his friend.
Then he felt bad, like he forgot Pebble.
Papa said, laughing is okay, Pebble would like you to be happy.
Toby smelled a flower slowly, and blew a candle.
Worried and brave can happen at the same time.

Death is the end of life for every living thing, and pets usually have shorter lives than people.
Sometimes a vet helps a very ill pet die peacefully so it is not suffering; this is called euthanasia, and it is a kind, loving decision.
Grief is the feeling of missing someone we love, and it shows how much they mattered.
Different families have different beliefs about what happens after death.
[[CHILD]] can ask [[GROWNUP]] what our family believes.
Vets and vet nurses care deeply about pets and often feel sad too.
Telling school helps teachers understand if you seem quiet or upset.
Some people do not understand how much a pet matters; that can feel lonely, and your feelings are still real.
Pet loss support groups and books exist because it is such a common experience.
[[CHILD]] can choose who to tell and how much to say.
Rituals give grief a shape and a place to go, which is why people have funerals and memorials.
Making something, like a photo book or a painting, can help when words are hard.
Some families bury a pet, some scatter ashes, and some keep them; each is a choice.
Anniversaries can bring feelings back, and remembering on those days is okay.
[[CHILD]] can plan a yearly way to remember the pet.
Grief is not a straight line; good and bad days mix for weeks or months.
Guilt, like thinking, I should have noticed, is common and usually not true.
Worrying about the death of family is a normal reaction, and talking about it helps.
If sadness stays very heavy for a long time, [[GROWNUP]] can find someone to talk to, like a counselor.
[[CHILD]] can keep a memory journal and add to it whenever they want.
Memory projects help the brain hold on to the good parts while the loss sinks in.
Writing a letter to the pet, saying what you would like to tell them, can help with unfinished feelings.
Some families donate to an animal shelter in the pet's name.
Getting a new pet is a family decision for later, not a replacement, and it is okay to wait.
[[CHILD]] can decide where the memory book lives.
